隋.note:
Yang Jian accepted the abdication of Emperor Jing of Northern Zhou in the 2nd month of 581, naming his state Sui, with the era name Kaihuang; the capital was Daxing City (newly built in 582 southeast of the Han Chang'an city and occupied in 583), and from 605 Emperor Yang built the Eastern Capital at Luoyang.
Emperor Wen: the Kaihuang Code and Statutes, the Three Departments and Six Ministries, the equal-field system and the grain-and-cloth taxes, the great census with personal inspection (dasuo maoyue) and the tax-assessment register system (shuji fa); in 587 he abolished Later Liang and in 589 destroyed Chen, ending nearly 300 years of division between north and south.
Emperor Yang: opened the Tongji Canal, the Yongji Canal and the Jiangnan Canal, launched three campaigns against Goguryeo, and toured north to the Turks and west to Zhangye; in 609 there were 190 commanderies and over 8.9 million households, the height of Sui.
After 611 popular revolts broke out everywhere; in 616 Emperor Yang went south to Jiangdu, and in the 3rd month of 618 Yuwen Huaji launched the Jiangdu coup and Emperor Yang was strangled; Yang Tong, Prince of Yue, proclaimed himself emperor in the Eastern Capital (era name Huangtai), and when Wang Shichong deposed him in 619 the Sui came to an end.

唐.note:
Li Yuan was the Sui Duke of Tang and custodian of Taiyuan. In the 5th month of 617 he rose in arms at Jinyang, in the 7th month marched south, and in the 11th month entered Chang'an, where he enthroned Yang You, Prince of Dai, as emperor (Emperor Gong) and made himself Prince of Tang; in the 5th month of 618 he accepted the abdication, naming his dynasty Tang, with the era name Wude and the capital at Chang'an.
Wars of unification (618–624, with aftershocks until 628): Li Shimin conquered Xue Rengao (618), Liu Wuzhou (620), Wang Shichong and Dou Jiande (621), and in 622 crushed Liu Heita (finally put down by Li Jiancheng the following year); Li Xiaogong and Li Jing conquered Xiao Xian (621) and Fu Gongshi (624); with the destruction of Liang Shidu in 628 the realm was unified.
In the 6th month of 626 came the Xuanwu Gate incident, and in the 8th month Li Shimin took the throne (Emperor Taizong), changing the era name to Zhenguan the following year. In 630 he destroyed the Eastern Turks and was honored as "Heavenly Qaghan"; he went on to destroy Gaochang (640), the Xueyantuo (646) and Kucha (648).
Under Gaozong (649–683), Su Dingfang destroyed the Western Turks (657) and conquered Baekje (660), and Li Ji conquered Goguryeo (668); around 669 (Zongzhang 2) the empire reached the Korean Peninsula in the east, the Aral Sea and beyond the Pamirs in the west, beyond the Gobi in the north and the northern border of Linyi in the south, the greatest territorial extent of the Tang dynasty.

陈.note:
Founded in 557 by Chen Baxian, who supplanted Liang, with its capital at Jiankang. In 579 it lost Huainan to Northern Zhou, and thereafter it faced the Northern Dynasties across the Yangtze; the Last Ruler, Chen Shubao (r. 582–589), indulged in wine and women.
In the 1st month of 589 the Sui forces of Heruo Bi and Han Qinhu crossed the Yangtze and stormed Jiankang; the Last Ruler was captured and Chen fell. Lady Xian of Lingnan then led her people in submitting to Sui.

后梁.note:
Xiao Cha proclaimed himself emperor at Jiangling in 555 with Western Wei backing; known to history as Later Liang or Western Liang, it was a vassal of Northern Zhou and Sui, its territory confined to the area around Jiangling, "300 li square".
In 587 Emperor Wen of Sui summoned its Last Ruler, Xiao Cong, to court and abolished the state; Xiao Cong's clan nephew was Xiao Xian, who later rose in arms at Baling.

高宝宁.note:
Northern Qi prefect of Yingzhou; when Qi fell he refused to surrender to Northern Zhou, held Yingzhou (modern Chaoyang, Liaoning) and allied with the Turks and the Khitan, and upheld Gao Shaoyi of the Northern Qi imperial house, then in exile among the Turks.
In 583, after Sui forces defeated the Turks, Gao Baoning was deserted by his followers and kin and was killed by his own men.

交州李氏.note:
The Jiaozhou magnate Lý Bí rose in arms in 541 and proclaimed himself emperor in 544 (the Early Lý dynasty in Vietnamese history); Lý Phật Tử carried on his cause, holding the area around Longbian in Jiaozhou and nominally acknowledging the Southern Dynasties.
In 602 Sui appointed Liu Fang expedition commander of the Jiaozhou route; Lý Phật Tử asked to surrender and was sent to Chang'an, and Jiaozhou came under Sui.

东突厥.note:
The Turks founded their state in 552 under Ashina Tumen and destroyed the Rouran; under Muqan Qaghan their realm reached the Liao Sea in the east and the Western Sea (the Caspian) in the west. When Sui was founded in 581, the qaghan was Ishbara.
In 583 Sui sowed discord among them: Apa Qaghan and Tardu Qaghan broke with Ishbara, and the Turks split into east and west. In 599 Tuli Qaghan (Qimin) came south to submit to Sui, which built Dali City for him; with Sui backing Qimin unified the Eastern Turks and became a Sui vassal.
Shibi Qaghan (609–619) grew strong again amid the Sui disorder and in 615 besieged Emperor Yang at Yanmen; the late-Sui contenders Liu Wuzhou, Liang Shidu, Dou Jiande and even Li Yuan all declared themselves his subjects and borrowed troops from him. Illig Qaghan (620–630) repeatedly invaded the south, and in 626 his army reached the Bian Bridge over the Wei.
In 630 Li Jing and Li Ji crushed Illig at the Yin Mountains; Illig was captured and the Eastern Turks fell. Their people surrendered to Tang and were dispersed south of the Gobi, where Tang set up the Dingxiang, Yunzhong and other area commands to settle them.

西突厥.note:
After the Turks split into east and west in 583, the line of Tardu and Apa held the lands west of the Altai Mountains, with royal camps in the Yulduz valley and at Mingbulak, controlling the lands north and south of the Tian Shan, Semirechye, the Sogdian states and the states of Tokharistan, and bordering Sasanian Persia to the west.
It was at its height under Tong Yabghu Qaghan (618–628), who "dominated the Western Regions"; Xuanzang met him near Suyab during his journey west. Later, internal strife split it into the Duolu and Nushibi divisions.
In 651 Ashina Helu rebelled against Tang, styled himself Shaboluo Qaghan and reunited the Ten Tribes; in the winter of 657 Su Dingfang defeated him on the Irtysh and the following year captured Helu in Chach, and Tang divided his lands between the Kunling and Mengchi Protectorates.

吐谷浑.note:
Founded by the Murong tribe of the Xianbei after they migrated west, with its capital at Fuqi City west of Qinghai Lake, it controlled the "Henan Road" of the Silk Road. In 609 Emperor Yang of Sui led a campaign in person; Fuyun Qaghan fled south to the Tanguts, and Sui set up four commanderies in his lands: Xihai, Heyuan, Shanshan and Qiemo.
Fuyun restored his state at the end of Sui. In 634–635 Li Jing and Hou Junji led a distant expedition; Fuyun was defeated and died, Tang installed his son Murong Shun and grandson Nuohebo, the Tuyuhun became a Tang vassal, and Princess Honghua was married to Nuohebo.
In 663 Tibet attacked and destroyed the Tuyuhun; Nuohebo fled with the remnants of his people to Liangzhou and later moved to the Lingzhou area.

高昌.note:
Gaochang under the Qu family (499–640), with its capital at Gaochang City (today the Gaochang ruins, Turpan, Xinjiang), was an oasis kingdom with a mainly Han Chinese population. Qu Boya paid court to Sui in 609 and married Princess Huarong; in 630 (or 628) Qu Wentai received Xuanzang with rich gifts and swore brotherhood with him.
Qu Wentai later sided with the Western Turks and blocked the trade routes of the Western Regions; in 640 Hou Junji conquered it, and Tang set up Xizhou in its lands, making Jiaohe City the seat of the Anxi Protectorate.

焉耆.note: Karasahr under the Long family, an oasis state on the northern route of the Western Regions. Guo Xiaoke defeated it in 644; from 648 it was one of the Four Garrisons of Anxi (Karasahr Garrison), and in the 670s Suyab replaced it.

龟兹.note: Kucha under the Bai family, a great state of the Western Regions, a center of Buddhism, music and dance, and the homeland of Kumarajiva. In 648 Ashina She'er and Guo Xiaoke conquered it; the Anxi Protectorate moved its seat here, and it was the first of the Four Garrisons.

于阗.note: Khotan under the Yuchi family, a great state on the southern route of the Western Regions, famed for its fine jade and its Buddhism. It surrendered to Tang after the Kucha campaign of 648 and became one of the Four Garrisons of Anxi.

疏勒.note: Kashgar under the Pei family, commanding the eastern foot of the Pamirs. It submitted to Tang in 648 and became one of the Four Garrisons of Anxi; it was later repeatedly harassed by Tibet and by remnants of the Western Turks.

高句丽.note:
Ruled by the Go dynasty, it moved its capital to Pyongyang in 427 (and to Jangan Fortress in 586) and held Liaodong and the northern Korean Peninsula. From 598 Emperor Wen and Emperor Yang of Sui launched four eastern campaigns against it (the defeat on the Salsu in 612), all without success.
In 642 Yeon Gaesomun killed King Yeongnyu and seized power; in 645 Emperor Taizong of Tang led a campaign in person, took ten fortresses including Yodong and Baegam, and turned back after being held at Ansi Fortress.
In 666 Gaesomun died and his sons fought among themselves; the eldest, Yeon Namsaeng, surrendered to Tang. In the 9th month of 668 Li Ji and Xue Rengui stormed Pyongyang, King Bojang surrendered, Goguryeo fell, and Tang set up the Andong Protectorate.

百济.note:
Baekje under the Buyeo family, with its capital at Sabi (modern Buyeo, South Chungcheong, South Korea), held the southwest of the peninsula; it was on good terms with Wa and a long-standing enemy of Silla.
In 660 the Tang general Su Dingfang and the Silla general Kim Yu-sin attacked together by land and sea; Sabi fell and King Uija surrendered, and Tang set up five area commands, including Ungjin.
Gwisil Boksin and the monk Dochim brought Prince Buyeo Pung back from Wa and restored the state from Juryu Fortress, with Wa sending troops to help; in the 8th month of 663 the Tang force under Liu Rengui crushed the allied Wa and Baekje army at Baekgang, Juryu Fortress fell, and the restoration failed.

新罗.note:
Silla under the Kim family, with its capital at Geumseong (modern Gyeongju, North Gyeongsang, South Korea). In the 6th century King Jinheung seized the Han River basin, opening a sea route to China. Under Queen Seondeok and Queen Jindeok it relied on Tang, and in 648 Kim Chunchu went to Tang to conclude an alliance.
Allied with Tang, it destroyed Baekje in 660 and Goguryeo in 668; in 663 Tang made its territory the Gyerim Area Command, with the King of Silla as area commander. Thereafter it fought Tang for the former lands of Baekje and Goguryeo (670–676).

倭.note:
The Yamato polity, with its capital at Asuka. It sent embassies to Sui in 600 and 607 ("The Son of Heaven where the sun rises sends a letter to the Son of Heaven where the sun sets"), and from 630 sent embassies to Tang.
After the Isshi Incident of 645 it carried out the Taika Reform, modeled on Sui and Tang institutions; in 663 it sent troops to help restore Baekje and was heavily defeated at Baekgang, after which it built water fortresses and mountain fortresses against Tang, and in 670 it changed its name to Nihon (Japan).

林邑.note: Founded by the Cham, with its capital at Simhapura (modern Trà Kiệu, Đà Nẵng, Vietnam). In 605 the Sui general Liu Fang defeated Sambhuvarman, King of Linyi, and entered his capital, and Sui set up three commanderies there: Bijing, Haiyin and Linyi; at the end of Sui, Sambhuvarman restored his state and sent envoys declaring himself a vassal.

真腊.note: Founded by the Khmer, originally a vassal of Funan. Between the late 6th and early 7th centuries it annexed Funan, and Ishanavarman built his capital at Ishanapura (modern Sambor Prei Kuk, Kampong Thom, Cambodia); in 616 it sent envoys to Sui.

骠国.note: City-states of the Pyu, with their capital at Sri Ksetra (near modern Pyay, Myanmar); Buddhist, and famed in Tang times for Pyu music.

堕罗钵底.note: A Buddhist kingdom founded by the Mon, on the lower Chao Phraya in today's Thailand; it sent envoys to Tang in 638 and 649.

天竺.note:
The states of the Five Indias. Between 606 and 647 Harsha (Siladitya) unified northern India, with his capital at Kanyakubja; Xuanzang took part in a great open assembly in his kingdom.
In 641 Harsha sent envoys to Tang; when he died in 647 his minister Arunasva usurped the throne and plundered the Tang envoy Wang Xuance, and the next year Wang Xuance, with troops borrowed from Tibet and Nepal, defeated him, captured Arunasva and presented him at Chang'an.

泥婆罗.note: A kingdom in today's Kathmandu Valley, Nepal; in the 7th century it was subject to Tibet, and Princess Bhrikuti married Songtsen Gampo; in 648 it sent troops to help Wang Xuance.

迦湿弥罗.note: A Buddhist kingdom in today's Kashmir Valley, where Xuanzang studied for two years.

波斯.note:
The Sasanian dynasty, which contended with the Turks for Central Asia. From 636 it suffered successive defeats by the Arabs; in 651 the last ruler, Yazdegerd III, was killed at Merv, and the Sasanian state fell.
His son Peroz fled east to Tokharistan and asked Tang for help; in 661 Tang made Zaranj the Persian Area Command with Peroz as its area commander, in reality only a nominal arrangement.

大食.note: The Arab empire (the Rashidun Caliphate, and after the 650s the Umayyad dynasty). In 651 it took Merv and controlled Khorasan, thereafter pressing steadily into Transoxiana; in 651 it sent envoys to Tang.

吐火罗.note: The small states on both banks of the upper Amu Darya (Warwaliz, Balkh, Khuttal, Bamiyan, Jibin and others); after the fall of the Hephthalites they belonged to the Western Turks, and a Western Turkic Yabghu was stationed at Warwaliz. In 661 Tang made the region into sixteen area commands, including Yuezhi, Tiaozhi, Xiefeng and Xiuxian.

昭武九姓.note: The Sogdian city-states: Samarkand, Bukhara, Chach, Kesh, Maymurgh, Kushaniya, Kabudhan, Khwarazm, Betik and others, whose commerce linked the Silk Road; long subject to the Western Turks. After 658 Tang set up area commands and prefectures there, such as Kangju, Dawan and Anxi Zhou, under the Anxi Protectorate.

拔汗那.note: A kingdom in today's Ferghana Valley, famed for its blood-sweating horses; in 658 Tang set up the Xiuxun Zhou Area Command there.

吐蕃.note:
The Pugyal clan of the Yarlung valley, which annexed Sumpa and other peoples between the late 6th and early 7th centuries. Songtsen Gampo (r. 629–650) unified the plateau, moved the capital to Rasa and created a script; in 641 he married Princess Wencheng, and he also married Princess Bhrikuti of Nepal.
It went on to conquer Zhangzhung (644), the Bailan, the Tanguts and other Qiang; in 663 it destroyed the Tuyuhun, in 670 defeated Xue Rengui at the Battle of Dafeichuan, and it contested the Four Garrisons of Anxi with Tang for over a century.

苏毗.note: A queen-ruled kingdom (Sunbo) around the Changtang and Nagqu in northern Tibet; conquered by the Pugyal in the early 7th century, it became an important part of Tibet.

羊同.note: An ancient kingdom around today's Ngari, Tibet, the birthplace of Bon, with its capital at Khyunglung Ngulkhar. Destroyed by Tibet around 644.

附国.n: Fuguo, Eastern Women's Kingdom and Qiang tribes
附国.note: The Jialiang, Eastern Women and other Qiang tribes of the western Sichuan plateau, called Fuguo in the Book of Sui; from time to time they sent tribute missions to Sui and Tang, and most were later absorbed by Tibet.

党项.note: A branch of the Qiang, spread across today's northwestern Sichuan and southeastern Qinghai. In 635 Tuoba Chici surrendered to Tang, which set up over thirty loose-rein prefectures under the Songzhou Area Command; the western tribes were absorbed by Tibet in the 660s.

白兰.note: A Qiang tribe living around today's Madoi, Qinghai, and the southern edge of the Qaidam Basin; first subject to the Tuyuhun, it was absorbed by Tibet in the mid-7th century.

爨.note: The Cuan, a great clan of Nanzhong, held eastern Yunnan (around today's Qujing, Yunnan) for generations. In 597 Shi Wansui campaigned south against Cuan Wan; at the end of Sui the clan again made itself independent; in 621 Tang set up Nanning Zhou, with Cuan Hongda as prefect.

洱海.note: The Wuman and Baiman tribes around Erhai Lake, among whom the Six Zhao, including Mengshe and Mengxi, coexisted; in 664 Tang set up the Yaozhou Area Command to govern them.

牂柯.note: The Zangke, Dongxie, Xizhao and other tribes of today's central Guizhou; from 621 they submitted to the empire one after another, and Tang set up Zangzhou and other loose-rein prefectures.

契丹.note: A branch of the Xianbei living in the basins of the Huang River (Xar Moron River) and the Tu River (Laoha River), a tribal confederation led by the Dahe clan. In 648 Kuge led his people to submit to the empire; Tang set up the Songmo Area Command, made Kuge its area commander and granted him the surname Li.

奚.note: The Kumo Xi, living southwest of the Khitan, around today's Chengde, Hebei, and Ningcheng, Inner Mongolia. They submitted to the empire in 648, and Tang set up the Raole Area Command.

霫.note: A small tribe living north of the Xi, subject to the Turks and the Xi.

室韦.note: Forest and steppe tribes on both sides of the Greater Khingan, divided into the Southern, Northern, Bo, Shenmoda and Great Shiwei, among others; in Sui and Tang times they were subject to the Turks, and the later Mengwu Shiwei were the ancestors of the Mongols.

靺鞨.note: Seven tribes: Sumo, Baishan, Boduo, Anchegu, Funie, Haoshi and Heishui; the Sumo and Baishan were subject to Goguryeo, and the Heishui were the northernmost and strongest; the Sumo later founded the state of Balhae (698).

薛延陀.note:
One of the Tiele tribes. In 627, together with the Huihe (Uyghurs) and others, it broke away from the Eastern Turks; in 628 Yinan proclaimed himself qaghan, and in 629 Tang invested him as Zhenzhu Bilge Qaghan; his royal camp was at Ötüken, with "200,000 fighting men".
In 641 it invaded the south and was defeated by Li Ji on the Nuozhen River; in 646 Tang and the Huihe attacked it from both sides, the Xueyantuo fell, and the Tiele tribes submitted to Tang.

魏.note:
The Wagang army was originally gathered by Zhai Rang of Dong Commandery (611), and Li Mi joined it in 616. In the 2nd month of 617 Li Mi seized the Xingluo Granary by surprise and opened it to relieve the hungry, styled himself Duke of Wei and besieged the Eastern Capital, Luoyang; in the winter of the same year he killed Zhai Rang.
Most of the contenders "south of Zhao and Wei and north of the Yangtze and Huai" attached themselves to him. In the 7th month of 618 he defeated Yuwen Huaji at the Battle of Tongshan, in the 9th month was defeated by Wang Shichong at Mount Mang, and in the 10th month surrendered to Tang with his remaining forces; at the end of the year he rebelled and fled, and was killed in the Xiong'er Mountains.

夏.note:
Dou Jiande, a native of Zhangnan in Beizhou, joined Gao Shida's uprising from 611 and gathered followers at Gaoji Marsh. In the 1st month of 617 he styled himself Prince of Changle, and in the 7th month crushed the Sui general Xue Shixiong at Qilijing; in the 11th month of 618 he styled himself Prince of Xia, and in 619 he destroyed Yuwen Huaji and moved his capital to Mingzhou, and all of Hebei was his.
In 621 he led over 100,000 men to relieve Wang Shichong, and in the 5th month was crushed by Li Shimin at Hulao; he was captured and beheaded at Chang'an. His general Liu Heita promptly rose in arms to avenge him.

郑.note:
Wang Shichong, Sui vice-governor (tongshou) of Jiangdu, was sent by imperial order in 617 with troops from Jianghuai to the Eastern Capital to fight Li Mi. After Emperor Yang's death in 618 he and Yuan Wendu and others enthroned Yang Tong, Prince of Yue (the Huangtai emperor), and he soon took power for himself; in the 9th month he crushed Li Mi at Mount Mang and took over all his forces.
In the 4th month of 619 he deposed Yang Tong and proclaimed himself emperor, naming his state Zheng. In the 7th month of 620 Li Shimin campaigned east and besieged Luoyang for eight months; in the 5th month of 621, after Dou Jiande's relief army was defeated at Hulao, Wang Shichong came out and surrendered, was spared, reduced to a commoner and banished to Shu, but before he set out he was killed by his enemy Dugu Xiude.

定杨.note:
Liu Wuzhou, a junior officer (xiaowei) of the Soaring Hawk Garrison (yingyang fu) at Mayi, killed the governor Wang Rengong in 617 and rose in arms; he submitted to the Turks in the north, styled himself Dingyang Qaghan and soon proclaimed himself emperor, and seized Loufan, Yanmen and Dingxiang.
In 619 he sent Song Jingang south, and between summer and autumn took Jinyang, while Li Yuanji abandoned the city and fled back to Chang'an; Song Jingang defeated Pei Ji repeatedly and took Jinzhou and Kuaizhou, and Guanzhong was shaken.
In the 11th month of 619 Li Shimin crossed the Yellow River on the ice from Longmen and encamped at Baibi, holding his fortified lines in a standoff; in the 4th month of 620 he pursued Song Jingang to the Queshu Valley and Jiexiu, fighting eight battles in one day; Song Jingang fled, Yuchi Jingde surrendered, and Liu Wuzhou fled north to the Turks and was later killed. His remaining forces under Yuan Junzhang held Mayi as dependents of the Turks.

梁师都.note:
Liang Shidu, of a powerful family of Shuofang in Xiazhou, killed the assistant governor in 617 and rose in arms; he raided the commanderies of Diaoyin, Honghua, Yan'an and Yanchuan, proclaimed himself emperor, naming his state Liang with the era name Yonglong, and submitted to the Turks in the north (Shibi Qaghan gave him the title "Dadu Bilge Qaghan").
He repeatedly brought the Turks south to invade. Isolated and without support after the Eastern Turks declined, he was besieged at Shuofang in the 4th month of 628 by the Tang generals Chai Shao and Xue Wanjun; his cousin Liang Luoren killed him and surrendered to Tang, and with that all the late-Sui contenders were gone.

郭子和.note: Guo Zihe seized Yulin Commandery in the 3rd month of 617, submitted to the Turks in the north and styled himself Prince of Yongle; in 618 he surrendered to Tang and was made area commander of Lingzhou.

秦.note:
Xue Ju, a local strongman of Jincheng, seized Jincheng in the 4th month of 617 and styled himself Hegemon-King of Western Qin; in the 7th month he proclaimed himself emperor and moved his capital to Tianshui. He held all of Longxi, with 130,000 fighting men.
In the 12th month of 617 his son Xue Rengao was defeated by Li Shimin at Fufeng. In the 7th month of 618 Xue Ju crushed the Tang army at Qianshuiyuan (Li Shimin was ill, and Liu Wenjing and others gave battle against orders), and in the 8th month he died of illness; in the 11th month Li Shimin fought again at Qianshuiyuan and crushed Zong Luohou, Xue Rengao surrendered at Zhezhi City, and Qin fell.

凉.note: Li Gui, of a powerful family of Wuwei, rose in arms in the 7th month of 617 and styled himself Prince of Great Liang of Hexi, holding the five commanderies of Hexi; in the 11th month of 618 he proclaimed himself emperor. In the 5th month of 619 his officers An Xiuren and An Xinggui (Sogdians) seized him and surrendered to Tang, and Liang fell.

萧梁.note:
Xiao Xian, great-grandson of Emperor Xuan of Later Liang, was Sui magistrate of Luochuan County. In the 10th month of 617 he rose in arms at Baling and styled himself Prince of Liang; in the 4th month of 618 he proclaimed himself emperor and moved his capital to Jiangling.
At its height his realm reached "Jiujiang in the east, the Three Gorges in the west, the far end of Jiaozhi in the south and Hanchuan in the north", with 400,000 fighting men. Later his generals grew arrogant, and Xiao Xian curtailed their commands and killed meritorious officers.
In the 9th month of 621 Li Xiaogong and Li Jing led the troops of Ba and Shu downriver on the autumn floods, and in the 10th month besieged Jiangling; Xiao Xian came out and surrendered, and was beheaded at Chang'an.

楚.note: Lin Shihong, a native of Poyang, succeeded Cao Shiqi as leader of a rising in 616 and in the 12th month proclaimed himself emperor at Yuzhang, naming his state Chu; he held the commanderies of Jiangxi, "from Jiujiang in the north to Panyu in the south". Later, under pressure from Xiao Xian, his territory shrank steadily; after 621 he fell back to hold the mountain caves of Ancheng, and in 622 he died of illness and his followers scattered and surrendered.

杜伏威.note:
Du Fuwei, a native of Zhangqiu in Qizhou, rose in arms with Fu Gongshi while still a youth, fought his way across Jianghuai, and in 617 held Liyang.
In the 9th month of 619 he surrendered to Tang, and was later appointed Director of the Southeast Branch Department and made Prince of Wu; in 620 his general Fu Gongshi defeated Li Zitong and took Danyang and Jiangdu, and in 621 he captured Li Zitong and held all of Jiangdong and Huainan. In the 7th month of 622 he went to court at Chang'an, leaving Fu Gongshi to hold Danyang.

吴李.note: Li Zitong, a native of Donghai, held Hailing after rising in arms; in the 9th month of 619 he took Jiangdu and proclaimed himself emperor, naming his state Wu; in 620, defeated by Du Fuwei, he crossed the Yangtze, took Shen Faxing's lands and held Yuhang; in the 11th month of 621 he was captured by Du Fuwei's general Wang Xiongdan, sent to Chang'an and executed.

沈梁.note: Shen Faxing, Sui governor of Wuxing Commandery, rose in arms after the Jiangdu coup of 618 in the name of punishing Yuwen Huaji, held more than ten commanderies south of the Yangtze, including Piling, Wu Commandery and Yuhang, and styled himself Prince of Liang; in 620 he was defeated by Li Zitong and drowned himself in the river.

汪华.note: Wang Hua, of a powerful family of Shezhou, held Xin'an at the end of Sui together with Xuanzhou, Hangzhou, Muzhou, Wuzhou, Raozhou and other prefectures, styled himself Prince of Wu and kept his territory safe and its people at peace for over ten years; in the 9th month of 621 he surrendered to Tang with six prefectures, and the people of Huizhou still revere him as "Great Emperor Lord Wang".

许.note: Yuwen Huaji, son of Yuwen Shu. In the 3rd month of 618 he strangled Emperor Yang of Sui at Jiangdu, enthroned Yang Hao, Prince of Qin, and led over 100,000 Xiaoguo guards back north; in the 7th month he was defeated by Li Mi at the Battle of Tongshan, fell back to Wei County, poisoned Yang Hao and proclaimed himself emperor, naming his state Xu; in the intercalary 2nd month of 619 Dou Jiande took Liaocheng, captured him and beheaded him.

燕.note: Gao Kaidao, a native of Tiao County in Bohai, first rose in arms under Ge Qian; in the 12th month of 618 he took Beiping and Yuyang and styled himself Prince of Yan, later making Huairong his capital. In the winter of 620 he surrendered to Tang, was granted the surname Li and made Prince of Beiping; in the winter of 621 he rebelled again, allied with the Turks to the north and repeatedly raided Youzhou and Yizhou; in 624 his officers Zhang Jinshu and Zhang Junli mutinied, and Gao Kaidao hanged himself.

罗艺.note: Luo Yi, a Sui Tiger-Brave general (huben langjiang), held Zhuo Commandery at the end of Sui and styled himself area commander of Youzhou, resisting Dou Jiande and Gao Kaidao; in 620 he sent a memorial submitting to Tang, and was made Prince of Yan and granted the surname Li.

汉东.note:
Liu Heita, a former general of Dou Jiande. In the 7th month of 621 he rose in arms at Zhangnan to avenge Dou Jiande, and within half a year recovered all the former lands of Xia; in the 1st month of 622 he styled himself Prince of Handong, with his capital at Mingzhou.
In the 3rd month of 622 he was crushed by Li Shimin at the Battle of the Ming River and fled north to the Turks; in the 6th month he returned with Turkic troops, and in the 10th month killed the Tang Prince of Huaiyang, Li Daoxuan, at Xiabo and retook Hebei; from the 12th month of that year to the 1st month of 623 Crown Prince Li Jiancheng, following Wei Zheng's plan, sowed division among Liu Heita's followers, and Liu Heita was defeated, captured and beheaded at Mingzhou.

鲁.note: Xu Yuanlang held Dongping and Lu Commanderies at the end of Sui, attaching himself first to Li Mi and then to Dou Jiande, and surrendered to Tang in 619; in the 8th month of 621 he joined Liu Heita, styled himself Prince of Lu and held Yanzhou, Yunzhou and other prefectures, eight in all; in the 2nd month of 623 he was defeated and was killed by country people.

宋义.note: Meng Haigong, a native of Zhouqiao in Jiyin, held Caozhou and Daizhou at the end of Sui and styled himself Prince of Songyi; in the 2nd month of 621 he was absorbed by Dou Jiande, and after Dou Jiande's defeat his lands passed to Tang.

冯盎.note: Feng Ang was a grandson of Lady Xian; the Feng clan of Gaoliang had long been chieftains of Lingnan. After Sui fell he returned to Lingnan, put down disturbances at Panyu, Xinxing and elsewhere, and held more than twenty prefectures, including Panyu, Cangwu and Zhuya; someone urged him to style himself Prince of Nanyue, but he refused; after Xiao Xian fell in 621 he sent his sons and brothers to call on Li Jing and submit, and in 622 he surrendered to Tang with his following and was made area commander of Gaozhou and Duke of Yue.

辅宋.note: Fu Gongshi, an old friend of Du Fuwei. When Du Fuwei went to court in 622, Fu was left to hold Danyang; in the 8th month of 623, falsely claiming Du Fuwei's orders, he rose in arms and proclaimed himself emperor at Danyang, naming his state Song; in the 3rd month of 624 Li Xiaogong and Li Jing defeated Feng Huiliang at Mount Bowang and took Danyang, and Fu Gongshi fled east and was captured.

隋余.note: Local commandery and county officials or strongmen at the end of Sui who held their own territories, still nominally loyal to the Sui (or to the Huangtai emperor in the Eastern Capital) and not yet under any of the new regimes.

安西.note:
Set up at Jiaohe City in Xizhou after Gaochang was conquered in 640; in 648, after Kucha was conquered, its seat moved to Kucha and the four garrisons of Kucha, Khotan, Kashgar and Karasahr were first established.
In 651, when Ashina Helu rebelled, it withdrew to Xizhou; in 658, after the Western Turks were conquered, it moved back to Kucha and was raised to a Grand Protectorate, governing the Four Garrisons and the area commands and prefectures west of the Pamirs.
In 661 Wang Mingyuan set up sixteen area commands, including Yuezhi, Tiaozhi, Xiefeng and Xiuxian, in the former lands of Tokharistan, and made Zaranj the Persian Area Command, so that its nominal reach extended west to the eastern border of Persia.

安北.note:
After the Xueyantuo were destroyed in 646, the Huihe (Uyghurs) and other Tiele tribes, more than ten in all, asked for Tang officials; Taizong made their lands into six area commands and seven prefectures, including Hanhai, Jinwei and Yanran, and in 647 set up the Yanran Protectorate to govern them, opening the "Road to the Heavenly Qaghan".
In 663 the Yanran Protectorate moved its seat to the Huihe tribe and was renamed the Hanhai Protectorate, governing the lands north of the Gobi; in 669 it was renamed the Anbei Protectorate.

单于.note:
After the Eastern Turks fell in 630, Tang settled the surrendered people south of the Gobi and in the Ordos Loop, setting up the Dingxiang, Yunzhong and other area commands.
In 650, after Chebi Qaghan was captured, the Hanhai Protectorate was set up at Old Yunzhong City (modern Tuchengzi, Horinger, Inner Mongolia) to govern the Turkic tribes south of the Gobi; in 663 it was renamed the Yunzhong Protectorate, and in 664 it became the Chanyu Grand Protectorate.

安东.note: Set up at Pyongyang in 668 after Goguryeo was conquered, with Xue Rengui as protector-general, governing nine area commands, including Sinseong and Yodong, 42 prefectures and 100 counties; in 676 it moved to Liaodong.

熊津.note: After Baekje was conquered in 660, five area commands were set up: Ungjin, Mahan, Dongmyeong, Geumnyeon and Deogan; after the Battle of Baekgang in 663 the Baekje prince Buyeo Yung was made area commander of Ungjin, governing the former lands of Baekje, which were gradually absorbed by Silla.

昆陵.note: After Ashina Helu was crushed in 658, Ashina Mishe was made Xingxiwang Qaghan and protector-general of Kunling, governing the five Duolu tribes east of the Suyab River.

濛池.note: In 658 Ashina Buzhen was made Jiwangjue Qaghan and protector-general of Mengchi, governing the five Nushibi tribes west of the Suyab River.
